A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AlienLM. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable matching across additions, removals, and relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, adaptation ablations, recovery attacks, seed-diversity experiments, and safety evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds generation evaluations, collaborative recovery attacks, data-volume experiments, and deployment measurements.

M1.justification: The vocabulary bijection, proxy representations, optimization objective, greedy pairing, client translator, AAT loss, and multi-key adaptation procedure remain unchanged. The additions evaluate or document the existing method.

E1.justification: Appendix D.8 adds TruthfulQA free-form generation and LongBench government-report summarization and paper question answering. Appendices E.3.5–E.3.6 add multi-user collaborative leakage and observer-tokenizer mismatch scenarios. Existing benchmark, coding, and safety coverage remains.

E2.justification: v2 Table 23, corresponding to v1 Table 8, adds white-box SentinelLM with gradient-based embedding alignment as an upper-bound reference. This differs from the retained black-box SentinelLM baseline. Table 1's comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include step-matched 50K/150K data subsets against 450K-pool checkpoints, with subset gradient accumulation of 2; generation evaluation using BLEU Acc, ROUGE-L Acc, and reported F1; and pooled-leakage budgets of 1K, 5K, and 10K pairs with shared versus distinct keys. These are added experimental settings, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.7 newly tests adaptation-data requirements. Appendices E.3.5–E.3.6 test whether per-user keys mitigate collaborative recovery and whether attacks depend on tokenizer knowledge. Appendices C.8–C.9 add serving-overhead and token-count analyses. Existing domain, alienization-ratio, seed, and safety analyses remain.

E5.justification: The existing five-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting and Figure 3 error bars are retained, including v1 Table 12 becoming v2 Table 25. No new repeated-run or uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented; the new serving results invoke measurement noise without quantifying it.

E6.justification: Matched original result tables retain their numerical entries. Added results include white-box SentinelLM's 62.39 average, data-ablation averages of 50.64 for 150K samples versus 51.80 for the full one-epoch checkpoint, and collaborative recovery of 6.05% with shared keys versus 4.40% with mixed keys at 1K pairs. New generation results show task-dependent utility losses and gains. Serving and tokenizer-sensitivity measurements are added; the qualitative examples at alienization ratios 0.2 and 0.8 disappear with v1 Figure 4.

T1.justification: The formal assumptions, bijection and translator definitions, round-trip proof, optimization derivation, and complexity analysis in Appendices A–C are unchanged. The added empirical evaluations do not revise these mathematical arguments.

C1.justification: The abstract adopts exposure-reduction and privacy-aware wording. The conclusion adds claims of negligible serving overhead and recovery of most full-data performance with 150K samples. The central API-only contribution and headline utility and recovery claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds qualifications that distinct user keys mitigate collaborative leakage at moderate budgets but do not eliminate it, and that generation quality depends on both task and backbone rather than answer length alone. It also cautions that token counts are not exact billing estimates. Existing formal-privacy, client-compromise, metadata, and safety limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 announces a code/data repository, describes CPU dictionary-lookup translation, adds token-count accounting, identifies GPT-5.1 and its judging rubric, and documents Hungarian matching and consensus thresholds for collaborative attacks. These extend the already substantial implementation documentation without establishing a change to the core implementation.

R1.justification: Related work adds Halawi et al. (2024) on covert malicious fine-tuning and connects its safety concern to AlienLM. Appendix D.1 additionally positions white-box SentinelLM as an empirical upper-bound reference. The broader research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Targeted edits revise the abstract, introduction, recovery discussion, and conclusion. Appendix E reorganizes O2 attacks into text and token recovery, and new experimental subsections are added. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is completely redrawn with an explicit user–translator–provider–model pipeline and token IDs. Table 3 expands and distinguishes recovery types; eight new result tables appear. Several existing appendix tables are reformatted or gathered on a later page. The full alienization-example Figure 4 is removed, while the shorter Table 2 remains.

improvement.justification: The white-box reference, generation evaluations, collaborative attacks, and deployment measurements make utility and privacy limitations more assessable than in v1. Added access and implementation information also helps reproducibility. However, Section 4.5 still states that O2 token recovery stays below 0.22% while its expanded Table 3 reports 6.05% and 4.40%. The broader evidence provides a net improvement, but this unreconciled security summary limits the gain.
